behavior_items: The program exercises Fortran 2018 coarray team features by importing `ISO_FORTRAN_ENV`, which provides the `TEAM_TYPE` derived type used to hold a team identifier returned by `FORM TEAM`.

`P` is a named constant set to 8, and `A [P, *]` declares a coarray with codimension bounds that make `THIS_IMAGE(A)` meaningful; the code uses the current image’s coarray index information to populate `ME`.

`ME` is a two-element integer array, and `ME(:) = THIS_IMAGE(A)` assigns the current image’s index information into both elements, so `ME(1)` selects the team-forming image and `ME(2)` supplies the new-team index requested by the standard example.

The statement `FORM TEAM (ME(1), ROW, NEW_INDEX=ME(2))` is the key reproducer: it asks the runtime/compiler to form a new team from image `ME(1)`, store the resulting team in `ROW`, and map the current image to the specified `NEW_INDEX` within that team.

gfortran 8.2 rejects this valid Fortran 2018 syntax during parsing, reporting `Syntax error in FORM TEAM statement` at the `NEW_INDEX=` portion, which indicates the compiler’s grammar or statement parser does not recognize the optional `NEW_INDEX` specifier in `FORM TEAM`.

The failure occurs before semantic analysis or code generation, so the bug is specifically a front-end language-support defect: the compiler cannot accept a standard-conforming `FORM TEAM` construct that includes `NEW_INDEX=` even though the bug report cites it as required Fortran 2018 functionality.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer is a minimal Fortran 2018 coarray program that sets up image-number metadata with `THIS_IMAGE(A)` and then invokes `FORM TEAM` to create a team while specifying `NEW_INDEX=ME(2)`. In gfortran 8.2, that syntax is not accepted and triggers an immediate front-end syntax error at `NEW_INDEX=`, showing that the compiler lacks support for this standard feature rather than failing later in semantic checks or runtime handling.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The failure pattern is consistent with a front-end language-support gap rather than a runtime or code-generation problem. Matches a member separator. With standard FORTRAN this is '%', but with DEC structures we must carefully match dot ('.'). Because operators are spelled ".op.", a dotted string such as "x.y.z..." can be either a component reference chain or a combination of binary operations. There is no real way to win because the string may be grammatically ambiguous. The following rules help avoid ambiguities - they match some behavior of other (older) compilers. If the rules here are changed the test cases should be updated. If the user has problems with these rules they probably deserve the consequences. Consider "x.y.z": (1) If any user defined operator ".y." exists, this is always y(x,z) (even if ".y." is the wrong type and/or x has a member y). (3) If x has no member y or (x->y) is not a derived type but ".y." is an intrinsic operator (such as ".eq."), this is y(x,z). Match a stop-code after an (ERROR) STOP or PAUSE statement. The requirements for a stop-code differ in the standards. Fortran 95 has R840 stop-stmt is STOP [ stop-code ] R841 stop-code is scalar-char-constant or digit [ digit [ digit [ digit [ digit ] ] ] ] Fortran 2003 matches Fortran 95 except R840 and R841 are now R849 and R850. Fortran 2008 has R855 stop-stmt is STOP [ stop-code ] R856 allstop-stmt is ALL STOP [ stop-code ] R857 stop-code is scalar-default-char-constant-expr or scalar-int-constant-expr Fortran 2018 has R1160 stop-stmt is STOP [ stop-code ] [ , QUIET = scalar-logical-expr] R1161 error-stop-stmt is ERROR STOP [ stop-code ] [ , QUIET = scalar-logical-expr] R1162 stop-code is scalar-default-char-expr or scalar-int-expr For free-form source code, all standards contain a statement of the form: A blank shall be used to separate names, constants, or labels from adjacent keywords, names, constants, or labels. A stop-code is not a name, constant, or label. So, under Fortran 95 and 2003, STOP123 is valid, but it is invalid Fortran 2008.
